purpose: IDS component API and state parity contract. Platform implementations may use native APIs, but public behavior must satisfy the same contract.

knownDifferences: Android filled-disabled uses a translucent brand tint; iOS currently uses a neutral divider background for every disabled variant.
Android destructive uses a solid danger container with white content; iOS destructive uses a danger-tint container and danger-colored content.
Web exposes additional secondary and success styling classes without an exact one-to-one native variant in the current contract.
Class or enum presence does not establish contrast, touch-target, focus, screen-reader, loading, or runtime visual equivalence.
semanticMappingAudit.completionGate: Do not mark cross-platform variant parity complete until each proposed mapping is reviewed against rendered light/dark screenshots, interaction-state tests, accessibility checks, and product-owner approval.

button.parityNote: Variant names and styling primitives differ by platform. The semantic mapping above is a review hypothesis based on source implementation, not proof of equivalence.

knownImplementationGaps: Android exposes explicit loading stateDescription and disables editing while loading; iOS initializer does not currently expose disabled or loading parameters; web styling supports disabled and aria-invalid selectors but runtime markup must provide those attributes.
Android and iOS expose error and success supporting text through component APIs; the shared web CSS only styles .tds-error and does not itself bind validation messages or accessible descriptions.
CSS styling alone does not establish screen-reader announcement, focus order, keyboard type, or successful runtime behavior.
textField.completionGate: Before declaring text-field parity, verify disabled/loading API behavior on all platforms, ensure invalid state is programmatically exposed, connect visible error text through accessible descriptions, and run keyboard plus screen-reader checks in light and dark themes.

knownImplementationGaps: iOS now exposes enabled, loading, and selected API states, with loading feedback and accessibility selected traits; visual parity still requires runtime review against Android and web.
Android announces loading in its row content description, while iOS exposes Loading through a progress indicator and accessibility value; announcement timing may differ by platform.

The web CSS styles active, focus-visible, aria-selected and aria-disabled states, but consuming markup must supply correct semantics and disable interaction; CSS alone does not make a row keyboard-operable.
listRow.completionGate: Verify pointer and keyboard activation, disabled interaction, selected-state announcements, loading behavior, focus visibility, and 44pt/48dp touch targets on Android, iOS and web in light and dark themes. Confirm rendered visual and screen-reader behavior before marking parity complete.

knownImplementationGaps: Android renders a text-first empty state and uses IdsButton for its optional action; iOS adds a decorative SF Symbol and uses a tinted button; web CSS supports icon/title/copy slots but CSS alone does not prove semantic heading or action markup.
Android message text fills the available width; iOS explicitly wraps multiline copy; web constrains copy to max-width 360px. Long localized strings need rendered checks at narrow widths.
The three APIs differ in icon support and action naming, so source-level presence is not pixel or behavior parity.
emptyState.completionGate: Render empty states with no action and with an action, long localized text, narrow screens, light/dark themes, and screen readers. Verify the action is a real accessible button and that heading/message reading order is meaningful before marking parity complete.

knownImplementationGaps: iOS ErrorCardView exposes a fixed Retry action; bank-mfe and merchant-mfe shared ErrorCard messages now use role="alert", but the two web components remain separately implemented and recovery behavior is not yet a single shared web contract.

Adding role="alert" covers the shared web error message semantics but does not prove announcements occur exactly once in every consuming flow; native Android and iOS announcement behavior and real screen-reader outcomes still require runtime verification.
Error styling and button treatment differ by platform; review contrast, recovery wording, retry loading/failure states and preservation of user-entered context in real flows.
errorState.completionGate: Verify recoverable and terminal errors, retry loading/failure states, preserved form context, accessible error announcement, keyboard/screen-reader order, and light/dark contrast on each platform before marking parity complete.

knownImplementationGaps: Android and iOS delay showing the placeholder by about 200 ms, while web CSS animates whenever the .tds-skeleton class is present; consuming views decide when to mount it.
Android uses a gradient brush, iOS uses a clipped LinearGradient, and web uses a pseudo-element shimmer. Similar motion does not establish equivalent contrast or layout.

Android checks the system animator scale and keeps the placeholder static when system animations are disabled; iOS checks accessibilityReduceMotion and web honors prefers-reduced-motion. Re-check whether native system-setting changes are reflected immediately while a screen remains mounted.
SkeletonBlock exposes a height and fills available width on native platforms; web sizing is supplied by markup. Verify placeholder geometry matches the content it replaces.
Android and iOS decorative skeleton shapes are hidden from the accessibility tree. Web markup must set aria-hidden=true on decorative skeletons; the CSS class alone cannot provide ARIA semantics.
The inspected source contract does not establish that loading announcements are announced exactly once; that responsibility belongs to the loading container or screen.
skeleton.completionGate: Verify layout stability before/after load, short loads that should not flash, live changes to reduced-motion settings, light/dark contrast, decorative skeleton accessibility hiding, exactly-once loading announcements at the containing screen, web aria-hidden markup, and real content geometry. Keep this component marked in-progress until runtime checks pass.

ios: public struct FixedBottomCTA<Content: View, CTA: View>

knownImplementationGaps: Android's FixedBottomCta pins the action below a weighted scrolling column but does not itself apply explicit navigation-bar or IME insets; the app window configuration and real keyboard/device behavior must be tested.

iOS FixedBottomCTA uses a ScrollView above the CTA and relies on SwiftUI safe-area and keyboard behavior; it does not explicitly document or configure keyboard dismissal, focus scrolling, or CTA behavior when the keyboard is open.

Web .tds-bottom-cta is sticky and includes safe-area padding, but it depends on the correct scroll container and a consumer-provided accessible button/action state; CSS alone cannot guarantee keyboard viewport behavior.

Platform layout mechanics differ (weighted column, SwiftUI VStack, CSS sticky), so equivalent behavior must be verified on long and short content, keyboard-open forms, small screens, and screen readers.
bottomCta.completionGate: Test one- and two-action CTAs, long and short content, scroll independence, virtual keyboard and system-bar insets, focus scrolling, disabled/loading states, accessible labels, and viewport changes on Android, iOS and web. Compare light/dark rendering and confirm no content or action is obscured before marking parity complete.

completionRule: A component is IDS-complete only when anatomy, variants, states, accessibility, localization, dark mode, responsive/platform behavior and recovery behavior are documented and tested.
